mainTopic: Are glowing coals (גחלים) considered 'fire' (אש)? Testing רבי's view that roasting the קרבן פסח on coals counts as צלי אש, against ברייתות about burns (מכות אש) and the coals of יום הכפורים.
overview: Earlier on the daf, רבי ruled that coals count as 'fire', so roasting the קרבן פסח on coals is valid צלי אש. The amud opens by finishing a side argument about the word 'ישרף'. Then רבינא answers a contradiction to רבי from the ברייתא of מכות אש by rereading it so that a coal is included in 'fire' from the start. רבא raises a new contradiction from the ברייתא about the coals of the קטורת on יום הכפורים. The גמרא first shows that this ברייתא seems to contradict itself. רב ששת rereads it, but his reading still treats coals as different from fire, which is a difficulty for רבי. אביי offers a reading that fits רבי, but רבה rejects it. רבא then gives a reading that fits רבי: the coals must already be coals at the moment they are taken from the מזבח. After a short note on how to spell עוֹמְמוֹת, a new משנה teaches what to cut away from the פסח if it was cooked by the oven wall or its own gravy, and what to do if it was smeared with תרומה or מעשר שני oil. The גמרא then begins a discussion of hot foods touching hot foods, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A verse is quoted against the previous answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a challenge by quoting the verse 'על שפך הדשן ישרף' about burning the bull outside the camp.
steps.simpleTranslation: [But it is written:] 'Where the ash is poured, it shall be burned'!
steps.whatsHappening: This line is the end of a challenge that started before our passage. The גמרא quotes a verse that contains the word 'ישרף', and the next step will respond to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger points to the word 'ישרף' in this verse, which looks like it could be used for a derivation in the previous argument. Because it looks extra, the challenger argues that the earlier reasoning does not work. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the ashes are poured out, outside the camp
It shall be burned

phrases.english: "Where the ash is poured it shall be burned"! (Leviticus 4:12)
phrases.notes: The exclamation mark shows this is a challenge. It continues an argument from the previous section of the daf.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: The previous argument about which word in the פסוק is available for a derivation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'ישרף' in this verse seems extra, so it should be available to teach something, and that undermines the earlier reasoning.

steps.title: The word 'ישרף' is needed for two other teachings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'ישרף' is not free for a new derivation. A ברייתא uses it for two laws about burning the bull.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: That 'it shall be burned' is needed for what was taught in a ברייתא. 'It shall be burned' teaches that you burn it even if there is no ash there. 'It shall be burned' also teaches that you must keep burning it, even after the fire has already consumed most of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends itself by showing that the word 'ישרף' already has a job. Since it is used up, it cannot be used for the challenger's derivation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a classic answer: the word is not extra, because it is needed for something else. The ברייתא learns two things from it. First, the ash pile is not required for the burning. Second, the burning must be completed fully, and burning most of it is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for. The word is used for a different teaching
As was taught in a ברייתא
The fire has caught most of it

phrases.english: They say: That "it shall be burned"
is needed for that which was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: ״יִשָּׂרֵף״ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין שָׁם דֶּשֶׁן.
phrases.english: "It shall be burned": even though there is no ash there.
phrases.notes: The ash pile is not essential. The burning is done at that place regardless.

phrases.aramaic: ״יִשָּׂרֵף״ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִצִּית הָאוּר בְּרוּבּוֹ.
phrases.english: "It shall be burned": even though the fire has consumed most of it.
phrases.notes: You must still finish burning it completely.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the verse in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The word is needed for another teaching (מיבעי ליה).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'ישרף' looked extra and available for the challenger's derivation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'ישרף' is used for two separate laws, so it cannot support the challenge.

steps.title: רבינא fixes the wording of the burns ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבינא solves the contradiction between רבי and the ברייתא of מכות אש. He rereads the ברייתא so that a coal is included in 'fire' directly, and only hot ash, lime, plaster, and fire-heated water need the extra word.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Combine the first two cases and teach the ברייתא this way. From 'a burn of fire' I only know a burn from fire or from a coal. If someone was burned by hot ash, by boiling lime, by boiling plaster, or by anything whose heat comes from fire, including water heated by fire, how do we know it counts? The verse says 'a burn', 'a burn', and the repetition includes them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives a new answer to the earlier contradiction against רבי. He changes how the ברייתא reads, so that a coal is part of 'fire' from the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the old reading, a coal needed the extra word 'מכוה', which suggested a coal is not 'fire'. In רבינא's reading, a coal is grouped together with fire in the plain words 'מכות אש'. Only things that are hot because of fire, but are not fire themselves, need the extra word. So the ברייתא now agrees with רבי that coals count as fire.

keyTerms.meaning: Combine and teach. Reread the text by grouping two items together
A burn caused by fire, a category in the laws of נגעים
Hot ashes mixed with embers
Plaster
Water heated by fire
It included. The repeated word adds more cases

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not adding a new law about burns. He is only showing that 'coal' belongs in the first clause together with 'fire', so the ברייתא never treated a coal as something other than fire.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבינא, a coal is 'fire' just like רבי said. Only things heated by fire need the extra word 'מכוה מכוה'.

phrases.english: Ravina said: Combine and teach:
"A burn of fire": I have only
one who was burned by fire or by a coal.
phrases.notes: This is the key change: the coal is now grouped with fire.

phrases.english: If he was burned by hot ash, by boiling lime,
or by boiling plaster,
or by anything that comes from the heat of fire,
to include water heated by fire, from where do we know?
The verse states: "a burn," "a burn": it included these.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new solution to the original contradiction against רבי earlier, in place of the earlier answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the text of the ברייתא (כרוך ותני).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to need a special extra word to include a coal, which implies a coal is not fire.
steps.terutzMaskana: A coal is part of 'מכות אש' in the plain reading. Only fire-heated substances need the extra word, so there is no contradiction with רבי.

steps.title: רבא contradicts רבי from the coals of the קטורת
steps.stepSummary: רבא cites the ברייתא on the coals for the קטורת on יום הכפורים. It says you must take glowing coals, not dying coals and not a flame, which seems to show that coals are not called 'fire'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised a contradiction: Did רבי really say coals are called fire? Here is a contradiction: 'Coals' might mean dying coals, so the verse says 'fire'. If it says 'fire', it might mean a flame, so the verse says 'coals'. How do we fit both? You bring glowing, flickering coals. This shows that plain coals are not called fire!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new challenge against רבי. He uses a ברייתא about the coals the כהן גדול takes into the קודש הקדשים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says 'גחלי אש', coals of fire. The ברייתא says that 'fire' alone would mean a flame, so the verse had to add 'coals' to teach that coals are required. That treats coals as something different from 'fire'. This seems to go against רבי, who said coals count as fire for roasting the פסח.

keyTerms.meaning: Raised a contradiction between two sources
And they contrasted it with. Introduces the contradicting source
Dimming, dying coals with no visible glow
A flame
Flickering, glowing coals with visible fire
This shows that. Introduces an inference

phrases.english: Rava raised a contradiction: Did Rabbi say
that coals are called fire?
And contrast it with this: "Coals": I might think dying coals,
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק in Leviticus 16:12, about the coals used for the קטורת on יום הכפורים.

phrases.english: therefore the verse states: "fire."
If it said only fire, I might think a flame,
therefore the verse states: "coals."
How so? He brings from the flickering coals.
This shows that coals are not called fire!
phrases.notes: This is רבא's conclusion against רבי.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא רָמֵי. מִי אָמַר רַבִּי גֶּחָלִים אִיקְּרוּ אֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new contradiction against רבי from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's ruling that coals are called 'fire', so roasting on coals counts as צלי אש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse needs to add the word 'אש' to rule out dying coals. That implies plain coals are not 'fire', which contradicts רבי.

steps.title: The קטורת ברייתא seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a problem inside the ברייתא. The first clause implies glowing coals are 'fire', but the second clause implies even glowing coals are not 'fire'.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: This ברייתא itself is difficult! You said 'coals' might mean dying coals. That implies glowing coals are fire. But look at the end: if it said only 'fire', it might mean a flame, so the verse says 'coals'. That implies even glowing coals are not fire!
steps.whatsHappening: Before answering רבא, the גמרא shows that his source has an internal contradiction. This sets up the next move, a resolution of the ברייתא, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half treats 'fire' as the opposite of dying coals, so glowing coals would count as fire. The second half treats 'coals' as the opposite of 'fire', so even glowing coals would not count as fire. Because the ברייתא is unclear on its own, it cannot yet be used as a clean proof against רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: But this source itself is difficult. It has an internal contradiction
Now say the latter clause
They are

steps.confusionAlert: This is not yet a final answer to רבא. The גמרא is only showing that the ברייתא needs to be explained before it can be used against רבי. רב ששת gives that explanation in the next step.

phrases.english: They say: But this itself is difficult.
You said: "Coals": I might think dying coals,
which shows that flickering coals are fire.

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא סֵיפָא: אִי אֵשׁ — יָכוֹל שַׁלְהֶבֶת,
phrases.english: Now say the latter clause: If fire, I might think a flame,
therefore the verse states: "coals,"

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא אֲפִילּוּ לוֹחֲשׁוֹת לָאו אֵשׁ נִינְהוּ.
phrases.english: which shows that even flickering coals are not fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבא by first showing that his source contradicts itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the קטורת ברייתא that רבא cited.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause implies glowing coals are fire, but the last clause implies even glowing coals are not fire. Both cannot be true as read.

steps.title: רב ששת rereads the ברייתא to remove its internal contradiction
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains the ברייתא this way. 'Coals' alone might allow either dying or glowing coals, so 'fire' limits it to glowing ones. 'Fire' alone might mean a flame, so 'coals' excludes a flame. Conclusion: take glowing coals.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב ששת said: this is what the ברייתא means. From 'coals' I might think any coals are fine, dying or glowing, so the verse says 'fire'. From 'fire' alone I might think a flame is fine, so the verse says 'coals'. How does it work out? He brings glowing coals.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת fixes the contradiction found in step 5 by giving the ברייתא a new, smooth reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In his reading, the word 'fire' is not what makes the coals count. It only narrows 'coals' down to the glowing ones. The word 'fire' by itself is understood as a flame, which is something different from coals. This removes the internal problem in the ברייתא, but it sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it [the ברייתא] is teaching. Introduces a rereading of a source.
Dying, dim coals that are going out
Glowing, still-live coals (literally 'whispering')
A flame
The verse teaches. Introduces a word in the פסוק that answers a possible mistake.

phrases.english: And Rav Sheshet said: this is what it teaches:
'Coals' — I might think either dying or glowing coals are fine,
therefore the verse says: 'fire'.
If it said only 'fire', I might think a flame is meant,
therefore the verse says: 'coals'.
How so? He brings from the glowing coals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the internal contradiction in the ברייתא raised in step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's two clauses seem to contradict each other about whether glowing coals are 'fire'.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both words narrow each other. 'Fire' excludes dying coals, and 'coals' excludes a flame. The result is glowing coals.

steps.title: רב ששת's reading still shows coals are not 'fire', against רבי
steps.stepSummary: Whatever the exact reading, the ברייתא treats coals as something other than 'fire'. That contradicts רבי, who holds that a coal counts as fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, coals are not called 'fire'. This is a difficulty for רבי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion from רב ששת's reading: the internal problem is solved, but the original challenge against רבי comes back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב ששת's reading, 'fire' on its own means a flame. 'Coals' have to be named separately. So coals and fire are two different things. This clashes with רבי's view, stated earlier on the daf, that a coal is included in 'fire'.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, whatever the details
Is called
It is a difficulty

phrases.aramaic: מִכׇּל מָקוֹם גֶּחָלִים לָא אִיקְּרִי אֵשׁ,
phrases.english: In any case, coals are not called 'fire',
this is a difficulty for Rabbi!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכׇּל מָקוֹם גֶּחָלִים לָא אִיקְּרִי אֵשׁ, קַשְׁיָא לְרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רב ששת's reading and shows it brings back רבא's original challenge from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's view that a coal counts as 'fire'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא, as רב ששת reads it, treats 'fire' as a flame and coals as something separate. So coals are not 'fire'.
steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת solved the contradiction inside the ברייתא, but that did not save רבי. These are two different problems: one about the ברייתא itself, and one about רבי.

steps.title: אביי's reading: 'fire' alone would include a coal, so coals are 'fire'
steps.stepSummary: אביי rereads the ברייתא. 'Coals' alone might mean only dying coals, so 'fire' adds glowing ones. 'Fire' alone might allow either a flame or a coal, so 'coals' excludes a flame. Conclusion: glowing coals.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: answer it this way. From 'coals' I might think only dying coals, not glowing ones, so the verse says 'fire'. From 'fire' alone I might think he can bring a flame if he wants, or a coal if he wants. So the verse says 'coals'. How does it work out? He brings glowing coals.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a different reading of the ברייתא that protects רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key line is 'if fire, I might think he may bring a flame or a coal'. That means the word 'fire' by itself already includes a coal. So coals are called 'fire', just as רבי says, and the difficulty from step 7 is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: Answer it this way. Introduces a new reading to fix a problem.
If he wants
A single coal

phrases.english: Abaye said: answer it like this:
'Coals' — I might think dying coals and not glowing ones,
therefore the verse says: 'fire'.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אֵשׁ, יָכוֹל רָצָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת — יָבִיא,
phrases.english: If 'fire' alone, I might think if he wants a flame, he may bring it,
and if he wants a coal, he may bring it,
therefore the verse says: 'coals'.
How so? He brings from the glowing coals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי against the difficulty in step 7 with a different reading of the same ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא proves coals are not 'fire' (רב ששת's reading).
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Fire' alone already includes a coal, so coals are 'fire', which fits רבי.

steps.title: רבה asks: where would a flame with no coal even exist?
steps.stepSummary: רבה quotes אביי's line 'he may bring a coal or a flame' and asks what a flame without any coal could possibly be.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: 'If he wants a coal he brings it, if he wants a flame he brings it.' A flame without a coal — how could you find such a thing?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה begins to examine אביי's reading by asking a practical question. This is setting up an attack on אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a flame comes from burning wood, so a coal is present too. אביי's reading suggests the verse must exclude a flame that has no coal at all. רבה wants to know what case that could be.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you find it? In what case does it happen?
Without

phrases.english: Rabba said:

phrases.aramaic: רָצָה גַּחֶלֶת — יָבִיא, רָצָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת — יָבִיא.
phrases.english: 'If he wants a coal he may bring it, if he wants a flame he may bring it.'
A flame without a coal,
how can you find such a case?

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁלְהֶבֶת בְּלֹא גַּחֶלֶת הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the practical case behind אביי's reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What real situation is a flame with no coal, the case that אביי's verse would be excluding?

steps.title: The case: a vessel smeared with oil and set on fire
steps.stepSummary: A flame with no coal happens when someone smears a vessel with oil and lights it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, he smeared a vessel with oil and lit it on fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבה's question by describing a real case of a flame without coals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Burning oil on a vessel gives a flame but leaves no coals behind. This is the only kind of 'flame' that אביי's reading could be excluding. The next step will show why this case causes a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, such as
A vessel, utensil
Oil
Fire

phrases.english: For example, where he smeared a vessel with oil
and lit a fire in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן דְּשַׁפְיֵיהּ לְמָנָא מִשְׁחָא וְאַתְלִי בֵּיהּ נוּרָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A flame without coal is a vessel smeared with oil and lit.

steps.title: No verse is needed to exclude something disrespectful even before a human king
steps.stepSummary: Such an oil-flame would never be brought before a human king, so all the more so before הקדוש ברוך הוא. The verse would not need to exclude it, so אביי's reading does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why would I need a verse to exclude that? Even before a human king people do not do such a thing. Before the King of kings, הקדוש ברוך הוא, surely not!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה rejects אביי's reading. The case it would be excluding is so obviously wrong that no verse is needed for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said 'coals' is written to exclude a flame. But the only flame without coal is a disgraceful oil-smeared vessel, which common sense (a קל וחומר from a human king) already rules out. So the word 'coals' cannot have been written for that, and אביי's reading falls.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need a verse?
To exclude
Now, if even (opens a קל וחומר)
All the more so

phrases.english: For that, why would I need a verse to exclude it?
Now, if before a king of flesh and blood
one does not do this,
before the King of kings of kings,

phrases.aramaic: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן!
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the case from step 10 to reject אביי's reading from step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי's whole reading of the ברייתא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It makes the verse exclude something that common sense (קל וחומר from a human king) already forbids, so the verse would be unnecessary.

steps.title: רבא's reading: the coals must already be coals when taken from the altar
steps.stepSummary: רבא rereads the ברייתא. 'Fire' teaches glowing, not dying, coals. 'Fire' alone might allow half-coal, half-flame, which turns fully to coal by the time he walks inside. So the verse says he must 'take' coals: they must be coals at the moment of taking.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: answer it this way. From 'coals' I might think only dying coals, not glowing ones, so the verse says 'fire'. From 'fire' alone I might think he can bring half coal and half flame, since by the time he goes inside it will all be coal. So the verse says: 'And he shall take a full pan of coals of fire from upon the altar.' From the moment of taking, they must be coals.
steps.whatsHappening: After אביי's reading was rejected, רבא offers a new reading that still protects רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבא's reading, 'fire' still includes coals, so coals are 'fire' and רבי is safe. What the verse excludes is a realistic mistake, not a disgraceful oil-flame. It excludes a pan that is still partly flaming when taken, even though it would become all coal on the way inside. The word 'take' (ולקח) sets the timing: they must be coals already when he takes them.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Drops the previous answer and gives a new one.
Half
By the time he enters inside (the קודש הקדשים)
Fire-pan for carrying coals
From the moment of taking

steps.whatToRemember: There are three readings of the ברייתא. רב ששת: coals are not 'fire', which is a difficulty for רבי. אביי: coals are 'fire', but רבה rejects this reading because it makes the verse exclude a disgraceful oil-flame no one would bring. רבא: coals are 'fire', and the verse excludes a half-flaming pan. The coals must be coals from the moment they are taken off the מזבח.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבא's reading keeps רבי's view that a coal counts as 'fire'. It also gives a practical rule for the עבודה of יום הכפורים: the כהן גדול must take coals that are already coals when he removes them from the מזבח.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said: answer it like this:
'Coals' — I might think dying coals and not glowing ones,
therefore the verse says: 'fire'.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אֵשׁ — יָכוֹל יָבִיא מֶחֱצָה גַּחֶלֶת וּמֶחֱצָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת,
phrases.english: If 'fire' alone, I might think he may bring half coal and half flame,
since by the time he enters inside
it will all become coal.
Therefore the verse says: 'And he shall take a full fire-pan
of coals of fire from upon the altar,'
from the moment of taking they must be coals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's rejected reading (step 11) with a new reading that still answers the difficulty against רבי (step 7).
steps.terutzResolutionType: New rereading of the ברייתא with a realistic excluded case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the verse, a half-flaming pan would be allowed because it becomes all coal on the way inside.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Fire' includes coals (fits רבי). The verse requires the coals to be coals at the moment of taking from the מזבח.

steps.title: How is the word for dying coals spelled?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the word for dim, dying coals is spelled with an א or with an ע.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: is it אוֹמְמוֹת with an א, or עוֹמְמוֹת with an ע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has been talking about dying coals. Now it asks a side question about how that word is spelled. It is setting up רבי יצחק's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a legal question. It is a question about the correct spelling of a word. The two spellings sound the same, so the Sages wanted to know which one is right.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the Sages
Dim / dying (coals), spelled with an א
Dim / dying (coals), spelled with an ע

phrases.english: It was asked of them (the Sages):
Is it 'omemot' with an alef, or 'omemot' with an ayin?
phrases.notes: Both words mean dim, dying coals. Only the first letter is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side question about a word used in the coals discussion of steps 8–12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The correct spelling of the word for dying coals: with an א or with an ע.

steps.title: It is spelled with an ע, based on a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק brings a פסוק from יחזקאל in which the same root is spelled with an ע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: as it says, 'The cedars in the garden of God could not dim it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers the spelling question. He quotes a פסוק that uses the same root, and there it is spelled with an ע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the word עֲמָמֻהוּ means 'dimmed it' or 'outshone it,' and it is written with an ע. This shows that the word for dim, dying coals is also spelled with an ע: עוֹמְמוֹת.

keyTerms.meaning: Dimmed it / outshone it (יחזקאל לא:ח), spelled with an ע
Cedars

steps.whatToRemember: The correct spelling is עוֹמְמוֹת, with an ע. The proof is the word עֲמָמֻהוּ in יחזקאל.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
"The cedars in the garden of God could not dim it."
phrases.notes: This is from יחזקאל לא:ח, and here the word for 'dim', from עמם, is spelled with an ע.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the spelling question from step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word is spelled with an ע, as in the word עֲמָמֻהוּ in the פסוק.

steps.title: Meat roasted by the oven wall or by its own gravy
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches what to do when the קרבן פסח touches the oven wall, or when its gravy drips onto the oven wall or onto hot flour.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the פסח touched the clay wall of the oven, he peels off that spot. If its gravy dripped onto the clay and came back onto the meat, he removes that spot. If its gravy dripped onto the flour, he takes out a handful of flour from that spot.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists cases where part of the קרבן פסח was cooked by something other than direct fire, and says what must be cut away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קרבן פסח must be roasted only by fire. A spot roasted by the hot oven wall is a problem only on the surface, so peeling off the outer layer is enough. Gravy that splashes back has cooked the meat with liquid, which goes deeper, so he must remove some of the meat underneath. Gravy that fell into hot flour has made that flour forbidden, so he removes a handful of flour from that spot.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (shortened to מַתְנִי׳)
The clay wall of the oven
He must peel off (only the surface)
Gravy / juices of the meat
He must remove (cut out deeper)
He must take out a handful

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'peel' (יִקְלוֹף) and 'remove' (יִטּוֹל). Peeling takes off only the thin outer layer. Removing takes away a thicker piece, because liquid soaks in deeper.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: If it touched the earthenware of the oven —
he must peel off that spot.
If some of its gravy dripped onto the earthenware
and came back onto it (the meat) —
he must remove that spot.
phrases.notes: He removes more than the surface, because the gravy cooked the meat.

phrases.english: If some of its gravy dripped onto the fine flour —
he must take out a handful from that spot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה. It continues the theme that the פסח must be roasted only by direct fire.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any part of the פסח cooked by the oven wall or by its own gravy must be cut away: peeled for surface contact, removed more deeply for gravy. Flour that absorbed gravy is taken out by the handful.

steps.title: The פסח smeared with תרומה oil
steps.stepSummary: If the פסח was smeared with תרומה oil, כהנים may eat it as is. For ישראלים, raw meat is rinsed and roasted meat is peeled.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he smeared it with תרומה oil: if the group is כהנים, they eat it. If the group is ישראלים: if the meat is raw, he rinses it off; if it is roasted, he peels off the outer layer.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a new problem: the meat was smeared with oil that is תרומה. Only כהנים may eat תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כהנים are allowed to eat תרומה, so there is no problem for them. ישראלים may not eat it, so the oil must be taken away. On raw meat the oil sits on the surface and can be rinsed off. On roasted meat the oil has soaked into the outer layer, so that layer must be peeled off.

keyTerms.meaning: He smeared it
Oil that is תרומה (only כהנים may eat it)
The group registered to eat the פסח together
He must rinse it

phrases.english: If he smeared it with terumah oil,
if it is a group of priests — they may eat it.
If it is (a group) of Israelites,
if it is raw — he must rinse it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם צָלִי הוּא — יִקְלוֹף אֶת הַחִיצוֹן.
phrases.english: And if it is roasted — he must peel off the outer layer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה continues with a new case: forbidden oil on the meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כהנים may eat it as is. For ישראלים, raw meat is rinsed and roasted meat has its outer layer peeled off.

steps.title: The פסח smeared with מעשר שני oil
steps.stepSummary: If the פסח was smeared with מעשר שני oil, the owner may not charge the group for the oil, because מעשר שני may not be redeemed in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he smeared it with מעשר שני oil, he may not charge the members of the group money for it, because one may not redeem מעשר שני in ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a last case: the oil was מעשר שני. It teaches that the owner cannot ask the group to pay for that oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone may eat מעשר שני in ירושלים, so the meat itself is fine. The only question is money. Charging the group for the oil would be like selling or redeeming מעשר שני inside ירושלים, and that is not allowed. He may only give it to them for free.

keyTerms.meaning: Second tithe, eaten in ירושלים
Money / payment
Redeem (exchange for money)

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה covers three problems with the פסח: (1) cooking by anything other than fire, which must be cut away; (2) תרומה oil, which is fine for כהנים and must be rinsed or peeled for ישראלים; (3) מעשר שני oil, which is fine to eat but may not be charged for.

phrases.english: If he smeared it with oil of second tithe —

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַעֲשֶׂנּוּ דָּמִים עַל בְּנֵי חֲבוּרָה,
phrases.english: he may not charge its value to the members of the group,
because one may not redeem second tithe in Jerusalem.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another forbidden-oil case. This time the issue is money, not eating.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He may not charge the group for מעשר שני oil, since מעשר שני cannot be redeemed in ירושלים.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that מעשר שני inside ירושלים can be eaten or given away, but never turned into money.

steps.title: The גמרא opens: hot food falling into hot food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a topic about forbidden foods that touch other foods. It starts with the case everyone agrees on: hot into hot.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: hot into hot — everyone agrees...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new discussion that grows out of the משנה. It is setting up a list of cases. It begins with 'hot into hot,' which everyone agrees about. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה dealt with food touching hot surfaces and liquids. Now the גמרא asks a general question: when one food touches another, what is absorbed? It opens with the clear case, a hot food falling into another hot food. The ruling that 'everyone agrees' on comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה (shortened to גְּמָ׳)
A hot item falling into a hot item
Everyone agrees

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished on this amud. Do not guess what 'everyone agrees' on yet. The ruling comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was stated:
Hot into hot — all agree
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא builds on the משנה's cases of food touching hot surfaces and liquids, and opens a general topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hot into hot is a case everyone agrees on. The ruling itself appears on the next amud.
